note.en: Left posterior cusp of aortic valve

steps.en: What you see: The ascending aorta runs long with the aortic root and outflow tract below. The cusps open and close in line with the vessel, and anterior cusp motion reads clearly.
Landmarks to confirm: Do not accept the view until each of these is on screen.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Each mistake below comes from the view catalogue with its correction.
Stenosis thresholds and continuity: Peak aortic velocity above 4 m per s means severe stenosis.
Mean transaortic gradient above 40 mmHg means severe stenosis.
Aortic valve area below 1.0 sq cm means severe stenosis.
Valve area by continuity equals outflow area times outflow VTI divided by aortic VTI.
Measure the ascending aorta at end diastole with the leading edge to leading edge method.

Pitfalls: Pressure recovery inflates gradients in a small root, so index the valve area and note root size before sending a moderate gradient for surgery. A high gradient with low stroke volume still means severe stenosis when the valve area is below 1.0 sq cm.

spot.en: Left posterior cusp of aortic valve
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Rib shadow cutting the valve in systole. Correct it by sliding half a space and timing the record for held breath out.
Off axis jet that understates peak velocity in stenosis. Correct it by fanning slowly and keeping the highest clean envelope found.
Right lung encroaching with deep inspiration. Correct it by recording at held breath out when the lung withdraws.

todo.en: How to get it: Place the probe at right sternal edge, second or third intercostal space, patient on right side.
Point the probe marker toward the head, about twelve o clock.
Nurse the patient onto the right side and press in the second or third right space. This window often gives the peak velocity that decides stenosis grading.
Freeze the image only when every listed landmark is on screen at once.

remember.en: Measure the ascending aorta for surveillance.

q.en: Peak velocity is 4.2 m per s from the right parasternal window only. What grade?

why.en: Above 4 m per s from any clean envelope means severe stenosis.

q.en: Root is 28 mm with a mean gradient of 35 mmHg and area 1.1 sq cm. What caution applies?

o.en: Pressure recovery in a small root may inflate the gradient

why.en: Small roots recover pressure downstream, so the gradient overstates severity.

q.en: How is continuity valve area calculated?

o.en: Outflow area times outflow VTI divided by aortic VTI

why.en: Continuity divides outflow stroke volume by the aortic jet VTI.

q.en: Gradient is high but stroke volume is low and area is 0.8 sq cm. What grade?

why.en: Low flow severe stenosis pairs a small area with a deceptively modest gradient.

q.en: Which patient position suits this window?

o.en: Right side down with the right chest up

why.en: Right side down brings the ascending aorta to the chest wall.
